rewrites.blindSummary:
This state/province is the country's most tolerant mainstream environment: 2026 travel guidance still describes a "live and let live" ethos, with gay-friendly life concentrated in several named districts, and no criminal enforcement against foreign tourists recorded. That informality, however, is not protection. The national penal code brought into force in 2026 criminalises extramarital sex, including same-sex relations; LGBTQ+ travel advisories rate this state/province "Exercise Significant Caution", public displays of affection are discouraged for all couples, and same-sex marriage remains unrecognised.

A 2025 ethnographic study of the state/province's trans women communities pointedly challenges the "refuge" framing, documenting persistent misrecognition and systemic discrimination beneath the tolerant surface. Visitors should read this state/province as relatively safer by local custom — with the new penal code, conservative local administration and documented structural discrimination setting the limits of that safety.
rewrites.blindTangential: Same-sex conduct provisions (the new national penal code's cohabitation and sex-outside-marriage provision) reach trans visitors in couples or shared accommodation, complaint-based but newly available as a leverage tool in any police contact.
rewrites.blindOutOfScope: The state/province's general tourism-hazard profile (traffic, surf, scams) is unrelated to trans risk; its relative safety is a social fact, not a legal exemption.
blindSourceSummaries: A peer-reviewed article (2025) on the 'precarious lives' of the trans feminine community in the country, based on four ethnographic case studies in this state/province: documents how trans feminine people navigate circumstances marked by both resistance and misrecognition and discrimination, challenging the narrative of victimhood while showing real precarity. For this record: academic ground-truth that this state/province hosts a visible trans community living with precarity, discrimination, and informal resistance.

A travel guide on this state/province: ranks the destination '6.3/10' with a legal score of 2.0, warning same-sex relations are criminalised in the country and that LGBTQ+ travellers face legal risks; advises visitors to 'keep your love a little quieter' despite its tolerant reputation. For this record: practical traveller-facing warning that the state/province's legal backdrop (national law) carries criminalisation risk even where the local scene is accepting.

A travel guide (Mar 2026): this state/province is broadly welcoming to LGBTQ+ travellers on a 'live and let live' basis, and same-sex relationships there are not a criminal offence under national law, though the new national penal code (in effect Jan 2026) adds complexity; same-sex marriage is not legally recognised anywhere in the country; several named districts are cited as the most consistently LGBTQ+-friendly areas with active venues, while public displays of affection warrant discretion. For this record: current, specific traveller guidance for trans/LGBTQ visitors to this state/province, including the 2026 penal-code law change.

rewrites.blindSummary:
No trans-specific legal measure or incident series is documented for this province in the surviving sources. The security environment, however, is not neutral: rights monitors recorded 138 acts of torture or ill-treatment in detention by police and military in the highland conflict zones between September 2021 and early 2025, "with almost no consequences", and a further surge of military deployments, fatal shootings and arbitrary detentions from August 2025, alongside internal displacement.

For any visitor — including a transgender one — contact with security forces in the highland districts carries a documented risk of arbitrary detention and mistreatment, and the surveillance environment raises the chance of being noticed and questioned. This is a general-population security finding, not evidence of trans-specific targeting.
rewrites.blindTangential: The new national penal code (Jan 2026) applies fully in this province; the region-specific factor is not an anti-LGBT bylaw (none found) but a documented security-force abuse pattern that worsens any police contact, including for gender-nonconforming travellers.
blindSourceSummaries: A monitoring-organisation briefing (July 2025): police and military in this province committed 138 recorded acts of torture or ill-treatment in detention in the highland districts (Sept 2021-Q1 2025) with almost no consequences; victims mostly males under 24 plus 7 women and 7 minors; arrests largely for alleged armed-group links or demonstrations; deaths during torture documented in operation areas; incidents catalogued on a monitoring database.

A rights-monitoring organisation's quarterly report Q3 2025 (31 Oct 2025) on this province: documents killings, arbitrary detentions, torture and the failure of accountability mechanisms by security forces expanding across the province, plus a healthcare crisis under scrutiny and arrests of protesters. Contains no trans/LGBTI-specific findings. For this record: indicates a high-violence, low-accountability security climate in this province relevant to overall traveller safety, but provides no trans-specific substance.

A general reference page: since June 2021 the country's home-affairs ministry has run outreach issuing transgender residents identification papers, and the page names this province among the provinces whose trans residents have benefited; only 'male' and 'female' sex descriptors are recognised, with birth-gender printed unless a court order was already obtained. The same page's national-framework facts apply in this province: the 2022 penal-code amendment criminalising sexual activity outside marriage (up to one year in prison) takes effect on 2 January 2026, same-sex marriage is not recognised, and customary laws may apply. For this record: evidence that trans people in this province may obtain identity documents through the national outreach programme, and the national legal framework a trans visitor stands under while in the province.

rewrites.blindSummary:
On 19 July 2026 the main city's government announced it was preparing a regulation rejecting LGBT, presented as local follow-through on Presidential Regulation No. 111 of 2025 on the national defence policy 2025-2029, which lists the 'spread of LGBTQ culture' among non-military threats; the mayor made the announcement in the courtyard of a grand mosque. The regulation remains in preparation, not enacted, with no specified penalty; no enforcement event is documented for this state/province. This state/province is one of the eight provinces analysed in a rights organisation's discriminatory-regulation mapping, and a neighbouring province saw a documented police raid on three trans women (November 2018) — the regional belt is where local enforcement is consolidating.

The deviation from the national score is small and below it, similar to a neighbouring province (0.13). The Presidential Regulation 111/2025 framing elevates local anti-LGBT measures from moral panic to national-defence doctrine — an August 2026 news report links the 'rule that deems them a threat' to a wave of street attacks on trans women, though it cautions the trend cannot yet be confirmed — but without an enacted local penalty the traveler-facing risk here remains prospective. It sits above a further neighbouring province (0.11), which has a live bylaw with specified sanctions.
rewrites.blindTangential: Presidential Regulation 111/2025's non-military-threat framing and the new national penal code (Jan 2026) apply to all visitors to this state/province regardless of the pending local regulation — the local fact is the announced rejection rule, the national facts carry the present legal exposure.
rewrites.blindOutOfScope: The main city's general urban-crime and traffic profile is unrelated to trans risk; the documented violence wave is in a different province and is used here only as the national trend context.
blindSourceSummaries: A local news outlet (20 Jul 2026): the main city's government is preparing a regulation rejecting LGBT, presented as local follow-through on Presidential Regulation No. 111 of 2025 — the national defence policy 2025-2029 listing the 'spread of LGBTQ culture' among non-military threats. The mayor announced the move in a grand mosque courtyard on 19 July 2026; the regulation is in preparation, no penalty specified, no enforcement documented.

A rights organisation's report: the mapping of discriminatory regional regulations in eight provinces includes this state/province, evidencing the state/province's place in the regional-bylaw belt that drafts like the main city's extend.

A news outlet (15 Aug 2026): an attack on a trans woman in a neighbouring city on 15 July 2026 was one of 10 attacks on trans women there between 30 March and 15 July 2026, with 45 victim-survivors per advocacy group data — victims punched, kicked, some stripped. The piece ties the wave to Presidential Regulation No. 111 of 2025 (effective October 2025) classifying the 'spread of LGBTQ culture' as a non-military threat, while quoting an official insisting it is a broader defence policy not aimed at LGBTQI people.

rewrites.blindSummary: No criminalisation of trans presence. The elected local legislature created an administrative legal gender recognition procedure in a 2022 Civil Code reform; after the Supreme Court struck down its adults-only limit in June 2023, a new reform passed in 2024 extended recognition to children and adolescents. In May 2022 the legislature also added a penal-code chapter "Crimes against Sexual Orientation, Gender Identity and Expression". The counterweight is a border city: the state/province's top government lawyer publicly warned of a serial killer of women in prostitution there (at least 3 victims; suspect arrested July 2023 after an international arrest notice and cooperation from foreign authorities), only 22 of 278 killed women in the state/province were classed as feminicides, and a 2021 burning of a trans woman's body in her home there is recorded within that pattern. Mixed: protective law, under-counted lethal risk concentrated in one border city.
rewrites.blindTangential: The border-city serial-killer pattern centred on people in sex work — victims' gender-nonconforming presentation is part of the targeting, so it reads as bias-adjacent violence, not pure criminal opportunity.
rewrites.blindLocalsOnly: The 2022/2024 legal gender recognition reforms and the penal-code hate-crime chapter operate on resident documents and prosecutions.
blindSourceSummaries: A rights organisation's country-wide tracker on legal gender recognition (March 2025), covering which of the 32 state/provinces have legislated an administrative procedure and the Supreme Court rulings that drove expansion. For this state/province: a 2022 Civil Code reform created an administrative legal gender recognition procedure for adults; the Supreme Court invalidated its 18-years requirement in June 2023; a 2024 reform followed.

A rights organisation's report (6 March 2024) on another state/province lacking a legal gender-recognition procedure: no such procedure exposes trans people to institutional mistreatment there — the August 2023 killing of an activist remained unsolved, hate-motivation provisions are absent from that state/province's criminal code, and healthcare staff routinely out patients by calling legal names. Baseline for how a non-reforming state/province behaves.

A news report (24 July 2024) on the national capital making transfemicide a crime with sentences up to 70 years (approved 18 July 2024), in one of the region's deadliest settings for trans people; over 95% of homicides nationally went unpunished in 2022.

A rights organisation's survey records that this state/province's elected local legislature enacted a 2022 reform to the Civil Code creating an administrative procedure for legal gender recognition for adults; in June 2023 the country's Supreme Court struck down the law's adults-only requirement because it did not recognize the rights of transgender children and adolescents; and in 2024 the legislature passed a new reform establishing a procedure for individuals under 18 and expanding legal gender recognition to non-binary people. This is the authoritative confirmation of the exact legal-recognition timeline the record states for this state/province.

A local news report (8 July 2023): a suspect was presented on 6 July 2023 in provisional extradition detention before a foreign judge, accused of the feminicide of a woman killed on 24 January 2022 in a hotel room in the border city's tolerance zone; probable cause was determined on 29 June 2023 by a foreign court, and he was arrested at his parents' home abroad, where officers found a hotel rent receipt and rope and gloves. At a 7 July 2023 press conference the state/province's top government lawyer called the 30-year-old a serial perpetrator, said extradition could take from 15 days to two years, and that nearly a decade of open case files were being reviewed; the investigation had linked him to at least three feminicides — one in January 2022, one on 14 February, and a 28-year-old killed on 30 August 2021 at a motel. This is the dated, local-press verification of the serial-killer counterweight in the record's border-city risk picture.

A local news report (8 March 2025): under the state/province's governor, 1,179 women have been killed in the state/province while only 110 cases were typified as feminicide — a small share that underscores under-classification of lethal violence against women — and female economic participation in the state/province stood at roughly 46-47%, 14th of 32 state/provinces. This state/province-level data supports the record's 'under-counted lethal risk' characterization, complementing the border-city serial-killer case.

rewrites.blindSummary:
No state/province-specific figures, articles or compliance records are supported by the vetted sources for this map. The national picture governs: by March 2025 an international human-rights organization counted 22 of the country's 32 state/provinces as having legislated legal gender-recognition procedures, with six state/province legislatures enacting none; a March 2024 report documents that where no procedure exists, trans people face police stops, denied documents and institutional mistreatment.

Transfeminicide has become a criminal category in some state/provinces — the capital imposes up to 70 years — against more than 95% homicide impunity nationally, and reporting finds convictions lag the statutes. For a visitor, this state/province's own documented record is thin: expect the country-wide picture rather than verified local protections or verified local hostility.
rewrites.blindTangential: The lethality ranking comes from national hate-crime tallies that count all LGBT+ victims together — violence targeting gay men and lesbians forms part of the state/province's numbers.
rewrites.blindLocalsOnly: The unremedied adults-only gap in the recognition procedure is a resident documentation problem; visitors carry nationally issued passports.
blindSourceSummaries: National framework (a rights organisation, 31 Mar 2025): legal gender recognition in the country is set state/province by state/province — as of March 2025, 22 of the 32 state/provinces had legislated an administrative recognition procedure, two more run one in practice without enactment, six legislatures have enacted none, and only seven state/provinces extend recognition to children. The country's Supreme Court set binding guidelines for the state/provinces and extended the right to minors in 2022; the regional human-rights court likewise requires a simple, accessible procedure. The organisation documents the consequences where no procedure exists (identity-document mismatch driving discrimination in schools, medical clinics and the labour market, incidents recorded in two named state/provinces). For this record: the national mosaic, not any locally enacted certainty, is the operative framework.

A rights-organisation report (6 Mar 2024) on a state/province lacking a legal gender-recognition procedure: without identity documents matching a trans person's gender, every document request or appearance scrutiny carries violence, harassment and humiliation risk, excluding trans people from employment, health services, education and financial transactions; context includes the Aug 2023 murder of a trans woman in a town in that state/province and more than 95% of homicides nationally going unpunished in 2022. For this record it is the operative evidence of what 'state/province law silent' means for trans people on the ground.
